rules.description: Fail only on a reachable, locally visible mismatch with a std raw-storage operation's documented preconditions: a raw slice exceeds its originating live allocation, assumed-initialized storage includes unwritten elements or invalid values, or ownership reconstruction uses the wrong original allocator/layout/capacity or creates a second owner. Trace the originating allocation, actual element type, offsets, writes/initialized count, length/capacity units, ownership transfer and cleanup. Give a concrete permitted input/path and the exact violated requirement. Do not duplicate obvious rustc/Clippy shapes such as directly zeroing an invalid type, directly forming a null reference, or publishing Vec capacity without any writes. Defects caused specifically by unwind belong to rust-unsafe-unwind-state; foreign pointer contracts and Python references belong to their dedicated rules.

levels: `source` makes no raw-storage publication, or every length is an element count, every reconstructed capacity is the original element capacity, and every element treated as initialized was written.
A raw-storage call is present, but `source` does not show whether the length is an element count, whether the capacity is the original capacity, or which elements were written.

A length is not an element count of the pointer's type, a reconstructed capacity is not the original element capacity, an unwritten element is treated as initialized, or a second owner is created for storage that already has an owner.

`source` contains a raw-storage call, yet it leaves the length's unit, the original capacity, or the set of written elements unsettled.

The length counts a unit other than elements of the pointer's type, the rebuilt capacity is not the original element capacity, an unwritten element is published as initialized, or storage that already has an owner gains a second owner.

rules.description: Fail only when visible std ownership/drop semantics and state transitions establish that a permitted safe callback, safe trait operation, panic, or forgotten restoration guard can leave cleanup, reentry or subsequent safe use accessing moved-out/uninitialized storage or destroying an owner twice. Trace raw read/move, published length, every owned local, the callback boundary, restoration and exact unwind cleanup. Treat arbitrary safe Fn/FnMut/FnOnce callbacks as potentially panicking; safe trait laws and Drop execution are not unsafe contracts. Name a concrete allowed callback behavior and the invalid state it exposes. Mere business inconsistency, resource leakage or lock poisoning is not a memory-safety violation. Do not invent custom destructor behavior or hidden guard semantics.

rules.description: Fail on a visible mismatch between a CPython/PyO3 raw-object-pointer contract and reference handling: from_owned_ptr(_or_err/_or_opt) consumes a borrowed reference without a preceding ownership transfer or INCREF; from_borrowed_ptr(_or_err/_or_opt) increments an already new reference without balancing the original ownership; a raw or Borrowed reference is used after its owning object may be released; or cast_unchecked/cast_into_unchecked is performed without an established compatible type check or construction invariant. Distinguish Bound::from_borrowed_ptr, which acquires a strong reference, from Borrowed::from_ptr, which does not. Trace the C API's new/borrowed/stolen reference semantics, null/error handling, every INCREF/DECREF and Python callback that can release an owner. Reference-balance mismatches are in scope even when the immediate effect is a leak. Missing semantics for an unknown foreign API are not evidence of a mismatch; known CPython APIs retain their documented contracts.
